articles.title: Quantitative Susceptibility Mapping and R2* of Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury Relates to Reactive Oxygen Species Activity.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Iron deposition following ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) plays a catalytic role in reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, contributing to myocardial injury and subsequent heart failure. There is a need for noninvasive imaging methods that quantify iron deposition and ROS activity post-IRI. We aimed to evaluate the relationship between myocardial iron content, measured by quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) and R2*, and ROS activity using PET. METHODS: IRI was induced in eight swine by percutaneous coronary artery occlusion. Three to seven days post-infarction, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was performed to acquire multi-echo gradient echo images to reconstruct QSM and R2* maps. ROS activity was quantified using a ROS-activated radiotracer [18F]ROStrace and corrected for myocardial blood flow. RESULTS: Magnetic susceptibility and R2* were significantly elevated in hemorrhagic myocardial regions compared to remote myocardium (susceptibility: 0.07 ± 0.08 vs. -0.03 ± 0.05 ppm, p value = 0.02; R2*: 43.9 ± 5.0 vs. 23.6 ± 5.6 Hz, p value = 0.0003). Infarct ROS activity was significantly higher than in remote regions (0.15 ± 0.04 vs. 0.11 ± 0.04 mL/g, p value = 0.0009). A moderate and positive correlation was found across R2*, susceptibility and ROS activity, with the strongest association between R2* and ROS activity (bootstrapped ρ = 0.59, p value = 0.073; uncorrected ρ = 0.65, p value = 0.02). CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates a moderate association between iron-sensitive MRI biomarkers in the myocardium and ROS activity in IRI. These findings suggest a relationship between iron-related tissue changes and ROS and highlight R2* and QSM as important imaging biomarkers, potentially aiding in the evaluation of therapeutic targets for treatment of myocardial reperfusion injury.

articles.title: Biparametric MRI with deep learning for the preoperative prediction of muscle invasion in patients with bladder cancer: a multicenter study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to develop and validate a deep learning model that integrates T2-weighted imaging (T2WI) and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) for the noninvasive prediction of muscle invasion in bladder cancer. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A total of 308 bladder tumors from 254 patients were retrospectively collected from three institutions. Of these, 177 tumors from Center 1 were partitioned via stratified sampling into a training set (n = 128) and an internal validation set (n = 49). The remaining two centers contributed 59 and 72 tumors, respectively, which served as external validation cohorts. A dual-branch 3D deep convolutional neural network (Joint model) based on biparametric MRI (bp-MRI) was developed using the training data and compared with a deep learning model based on T2WI (T2WI model) and VI-RADS assessments by radiologists. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. RESULTS: The Joint model achieved mean AUCs of 0.979 ± 0.007 in the internal validation cohort, and 0.907 ± 0.013 and 0.916 ± 0.021 in the external validation cohorts. It outperformed the T2WI model in all cohorts and achieved higher AUCs than radiologists across all validation cohorts. Notably, for equivocal VI-RADS 2-3 lesions, the Joint model yielded higher accuracy than the T2WI model in external validation. CONCLUSION: Compared with the T2WI model and VI-RADS assessment, the Joint model demonstrated better diagnostic performance and generalizability for predicting muscle invasion in patients with bladder cancer. KEY POINTS: Question Reliable noninvasive tools for preoperative prediction of muscle invasion in bladder cancer are lacking, as TURBT-based staging carries procedural risks and frequent understaging. Findings A biparametric MRI deep learning model achieved AUCs of 0.907-0.979 across internal and external validation cohorts, outperforming T2WI-only models and VI-RADS. Critical relevance statement Contrast-free biparametric MRI combined with deep learning enables accurate, generalizable preoperative prediction of muscle invasion, offering particular value for equivocal VI-RADS 2-3 lesions and supporting noninvasive clinical decision-making.

articles.title: DicomDoodle: Human-in-the-Loop Annotation of 3D MRI DICOM Images with AI Support and DICOM-SEG Compatibility.
articles.abstract: Accurate medical image annotation requires curation and remains a major bottleneck due to its time-intensive nature and inter-observer variability. To address this, we developed DicomDoodle, an open-source, Python-based tool for human-in-the-loop annotation that integrates a fine-tuned YOLO11 detector with the Segment Anything Model (SAM) 2.1 for prompt-based segmentation, alongside manual annotation and correction tools. DicomDoodle saves annotations as DICOM Segmentation (DICOM-SEG) objects, which passed automated structural conformance testing (22 checks across all 122 series) and were successfully imported and rendered in OHIF Viewer. Annotation performance was evaluated using brain MRIs from 37 patients (122 series) across three Indian hospitals, with the patient as the unit of analysis. SAM 2.1 and SAM 3 performed best among the six benchmarked SAM and MEDSAM models. Patient-level mean slice and volume IoU were poor for the fully automated workflow, at 0.109 (95% confidence interval 0.087-0.130) and 0.133 (0.102-0.164), respectively, revealing its limitations. It improved to 0.388 (0.329-0.446) and 0.338 (0.280-0.396) with slice-range prompting, and 0.858 (0.841-0.875) and 0.865 (0.843-0.886) with per-slice bounding-box prompting. For complete, unfiltered volumes, the automated workflow detected 95% of slices containing lesions. Still, it labeled about 90% of lesion-free slices as lesion-present; prompting removed almost all of these false positives. Segmentation accuracy did not degrade with lesion extent. In routine use, annotation sessions were provisionally estimated as shorter than a fixed manual reference. DicomDoodle offers an accessible, open-source platform that combines AI-assisted prompting with native DICOM-SEG generation to assist annotation.

articles.title: CASSFormer: A Lightweight CNN-Transformer Hybrid Network for Real-Time Coronary Artery Stenosis Detection and Localization.
articles.abstract: Coronary angiography (CAG) is the clinical gold standard for assessing coronary artery stenosis. However, its two-dimensional projection nature often causes vessel overlap and limited contrast, making subtle or complex stenotic regions difficult to detect and localize, thereby increasing reliance on experienced cardiologists. Existing deep learning methods face a practical trade-off: CNN-based models struggle with low-contrast or small-scale lesions, while Transformer-based models incur high computational cost, limiting real-time applicability. To address these challenges, we propose Coronary Angiography Structure-aware Stenosis Transformer (CASSFormer), a lightweight CNN-Transformer hybrid network for real-time coronary artery stenosis detection and localization. Specifically, CASSFormer integrates three key components: (i) a multi-stage spatial feature downsampling module (MSFD) to preserve fine-grained vascular textures during early feature extraction; (ii) a multi-scale mixed-topology block (MMTB) to model elongated vessel structures and multi-scale stenotic patterns; (iii) a dual-attention cross-scale adaptive fusion module (DCAF) that jointly exploits local directional attention and global channel attention to enhance sensitivity to low-contrast and small-scale stenotic regions. Experiments on a large private clinical dataset and two public datasets (ARCADE, ADSD) show that CASSFormer achieves favorable detection and localization performance compared with mainstream detection models, while maintaining low computational overhead (27.1 GFLOPs, 11.9M parameters) and an average inference time of 8.0 ms per image. Visualization results further suggest its robustness under challenging angiographic conditions, including vessel overlap, distal small vessels, and severe stenosis or vessel interruption associated with myocardial infarction. These results support CASSFormer as an efficient assistive tool for stenosis detection and localization in complex CAG scenarios.

articles.title: SAK-YOLO: An Improved YOLOv11-Based Method for Coronary Artery Stenosis Segmentation and Grading Judgment.
articles.abstract: Exposure to low-temperature environments predisposes to coronary spasm and plaque rupture, raising acute myocardial infarction risk. Coronary angiography is the principal diagnostic modality, but image noise, low contrast and poor vessel visualisation frequently cause missed detection. Conventional segmentation approaches depend heavily on expert input, while existing deep learning models remain limited in extracting multi-scale stenotic features and in grading stenosis severity. This study proposes SAK-YOLO, built on YOLOv11-seg with Switchable Atrous Convolution (SAConv) and KernelWarehouse dynamic convolution. A four-tier stenosis grading dataset was established from 376 angiographic images of 122 patients, augmented by flipping, rotation and contrast adjustment. SAConv replaces the backbone's strided convolutions to adapt the receptive field to varying vessel calibres, while KWConv and KW3K2 replace the neck convolutions, assembling kernels from a small warehouse of candidates. SAK-YOLO attains a box precision of 0.946, a box recall of 0.853, box mAP50 and mAP50-95 of 92.7% and 75.3%, and mask mAP50 and mask mAP50-95 of 91.3% and 56.5%, achieving the best result among all evaluated models on every mAP-based metric. These results indicate that SAK-YOLO has potential for coronary stenosis image analysis; however, they are based on a relatively small single-centre dataset, and multi-centre validation and prospective clinical evaluation are still required to establish its generalizability and clinical value.

articles.title: HDFF-Net: A Hybrid Dual-Feature Fusion Network with Bidirectional Gated Fusion for Colposcopic Transformation Zone Classification, Evaluated under a Leakage-Audited Cluster-Level Protocol.
articles.abstract: Cervical cancer screening through colposcopy depends critically on accurate classification of the transformation zone (TZ) according to the 2011 IFCPC nomenclature, as TZ type directly governs treatment eligibility (ablative versus excisional). Inter-rater agreement among trained colposcopists for TZ-type assignment is only κ ≈ 0.42-0.60, well below the κ ≥ 0.80 threshold considered reliable for clinical decision-making. Existing automated methods rely either on handcrafted feature pipelines or deep transfer learning in isolation, and published performance figures on public colposcopy atlases have not been systematically audited for evaluation integrity. This paper reports a leakage-audited, cluster-level evaluation of a hybrid handcrafted-plus-deep fusion design on a public colposcopy atlas and asks whether the fusion adds value over simpler baselines when only a few hundred images are available. We evaluate HDFF-Net (Hybrid Dual-Feature Fusion Network), a dual-stream design that combines a 10,322-dimensional multi-scale handcrafted feature branch (MS-GLCM, MS-LBP, MS-HOG), projected to 512 dimensions and recalibrated by a 1D Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) module, with an EfficientNet branch augmented by CBAM. The two streams are joined by a bidirectional gated fusion (BGF) module that uses feature-wise sigmoid gates; it is not an attention mechanism (no query-key interaction, softmax, attention heads or spatial tokens). Models are trained on a stratified 70/15/15 split made at the level of 194 unique image clusters (seed = 42), obtained by perceptual-hash deduplication (pHash, Hamming distance <= 8) of 366 IARC Cervical Screening Atlas files. Alias files of one cluster are the same physical image, so the primary analysis uses one observation per cluster; all intervals and paired tests are computed at that level and file-level figures are given only as a sensitivity analysis. Ablations compare handcrafted-only, CNN-only, concatenation and gated-fusion variants, and recent CNN and hybrid-feature baselines were retrained on the same locked split. Deduplication reduced 366 files to 194 unique image clusters (120 TZ1/34 TZ2/40 TZ3) after removal of seven label-contradictory clusters. The held-out test partition contains 30 independent clusters (53 files). On these 30 clusters, HDFF-Net (B0) reached accuracy 0.467 (0.283-0.657), balanced accuracy 0.420 (0.204-0.653) and macro-F1 0.407 (0.217-0.585). Ten baselines were compared with it on the same clusters. MobileNetV3-Large had the highest balanced accuracy (0.636 (0.424-0.855)), but no comparator differed significantly from HDFF-Net after Holm correction (smallest adjusted p = 0.386, MobileNetV3; unadjusted exact McNemar p = 0.039), and the intervals overlap broadly: with 30 clusters the study can detect only large differences. HDFF-Net overfitted (training accuracy 100%, validation accuracy 65-71%). In the ablation (five seeds), replacing concatenation by gated fusion changed balanced accuracy by - 0.031 (95% CI - 0.113 to + 0.048; exact p = 1.000), SE gating by + 0.005 (95% CI - 0.044 to + 0.070; exact p = 1.000) and CBAM by + 0.024 (95% CI - 0.049 to + 0.087; exact p = 1.000); the CNN-only variants had higher mean balanced accuracy (0.555 ± 0.065 and 0.579 ± 0.032) than the full fusion model (0.440 ± 0.118). In five-fold cluster-level cross-validation on 194 clusters, all five models tested reached pooled balanced accuracy of only 0.395-0.431 (chance 0.333) with overlapping intervals (Table 10). HDFF-Net is assembled from established components (SE gating, CBAM, an EfficientNet backbone and sigmoid gated fusion). In this study it did not outperform simpler baselines, and neither the gated fusion nor the SE and CBAM modules showed a measurable benefit; it is therefore reported as a negative result, not as an improvement over the state of the art. The contributions supported by the data are: (1) an audit showing that resample-before-split contamination and alias-file leakage in the IARC atlas inflated accuracy from roughly 49-76% to 99%; (2) a cluster-level evaluation protocol with all inference at the level of independent observations; (3) a controlled comparison of handcrafted-only, CNN-only, concatenation and gated-fusion variants, which found no benefit of fusion at this sample size; and (4) documentation of dataset provenance and label uncertainty. With 194 unique images, a single internal split and no external validation, the results support no claim of superiority, generalisability or clinical readiness.

articles.title: Availability-Aware Prediction of CCTA Findings Using Opportunistic Low-Dose CT and Routine Health-Check Data.
articles.abstract: Laboratory and history data are inconsistently available in health-check records, complicating prediction from combined clinical and imaging inputs. We evaluated an availability-aware ensemble for predicting coronary CT angiography (CCTA) findings in 864 participants, including 221 with Coronary Artery Disease Reporting and Data System (CAD-RADS) category ≥ 3. Models used eight clinical and 31 low-dose CT (LDCT) inputs, with optional laboratory and history variables. Six learner families underwent fivefold outer and fivefold inner validation; preprocessing, model selection, and cross-fitted sigmoid calibration were confined to outer training data. Calibrated adaptive top-3 aggregation achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.808, average precision of 0.622, and Brier score of 0.14152. Compared with selection of one compatible model, the AUROC difference was + 0.0193 (conditional 95% confidence interval 0.0029-0.0358) and the Brier difference was - 0.01174 (- 0.01723 to - 0.00621). Comparisons with the expanded-pool imputation baseline and common-feature ensembles were inconclusive. Matched analyses supported adding laboratory variables to single-model selection; history increments were uncertain. At threshold 0.15, 29/221 positive cases were missed (13.1%; 95% Wilson interval 9.3-18.2%). Human reviewers considered the proxy measurements acceptable in all 864 analyzed participants. Aggregation improved AUROC and Brier score relative to compatible single-model selection in this cohort. Its additional value over simpler ensembles and its suitability for clinical triage require external and prospective evaluation.

articles.title: From Dictation to Structured Report: A Multicenter Evaluation of a Large Language Model-Assisted Dictation and Report Structuring Workflow in Radiological Reporting.
articles.abstract: The conventional dictation-transcription workflow may delay report draft readiness and is susceptible to operational errors, including the inadvertent deletion of normal baseline statements from the template. This study compared a large language model (LLM)-assisted speech-to-text conversion and template placement workflow with conventional transcription. In a controlled retrospective workflow simulation, 450 contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography (CT) examinations from three centers (one radiologist-transcriptionist pair each) were re-dictated. Using the same Turkish audio recording and standard template, 900 paired report drafts were produced. Drafts were scored on a 5-point Likert scale by the dictating radiologist, who was not informed of the workflow of origin; no independent reference-standard comparison was performed. The overall Findings-section score, reflecting perceived linguistic and structural quality, was 3.19 ± 0.49 in the conventional and 4.39 ± 0.27 in the LLM arm (difference 1.20; 95% confidence interval 1.15-1.24; p < 0.001), with the largest difference in spelling/grammar. Inadvertent deletion of normal baseline statements decreased from 192/450 (42.7%) to 32/450 (7.1%) drafts (risk difference 35.6%; p < 0.001). Time to draft readiness, including queue waiting in the conventional arm, was a median of 34.5 versus 1.00 min (p < 0.001). LLM-assisted drafts had higher perceived linguistic and structural quality, fewer deletions of normal baseline statements, and earlier availability for review. Because clinical fidelity was not independently verified and correction time was not measured, these findings do not establish improved report accuracy or end-to-end efficiency and warrant prospective evaluation with independent evaluators, with radiologist final approval maintained.

articles.title: Feasibility of Simulated Low-Dose CT with Deep Learning Denoising for Lymphoma PET/CT Imaging: A Clinical Study on Lesion Detection, Staging, and Therapy Response.
articles.abstract: [18F]FDG PET/CT is central to lymphoma staging and treatment-response assessment, but repeated examinations increase cumulative radiation exposure, largely from the CT component. This retrospective study included 152 patients with 211 whole-body PET/CT scans and evaluated whether deep learning-denoised simulated low-dose CT can preserve diagnostic performance. A single-scan cohort of 108 patients was used exclusively for model development, while an independent follow-up cohort of 44 patients (103 examinations) was reserved for quantitative evaluation and a fully crossed multi-reader, multi-case study. Simulated low-dose CT images ranging from 2/3 to 1/8 of the standard dose were reviewed, and the 1/4-dose level was selected as the lowest clinically acceptable level. A denoising model was trained using paired standard-dose CT (SDCT) and simulated low-dose CT at 1/4 of the standard dose (SLDCT) images. Six nuclear medicine physicians evaluated three imaging conditions: PET/CT with SDCT, PET/CT with SLDCT, and PET/CT with denoised SLDCT (D-SLDCT), for image quality, lesion detectability, staging, and treatment response. D-SLDCT significantly improved quantitative image quality compared with SLDCT (all p < 0.0001) and increased subjective image-quality scores (4.11 ± 0.46 vs 3.00 ± 0.00). Staging accuracy was lower under the SLDCT condition than under the SDCT condition (MAE, 1.50 ± 0.27 vs 1.40 ± 0.20; p = 0.0011), whereas the D-SLDCT condition did not differ significantly from the SDCT condition (MAE, 1.44 ± 0.22; p = 0.47). Differences were more pronounced in patients with BMI ≥ 24 kg/m2 and among junior readers. Lesion detectability and treatment-response assessment did not differ significantly across conditions, while within-reader lesion-detection agreement with the SDCT condition improved after denoising (κ = 0.72 vs 0.67). The D-SLDCT condition preserved diagnostic performance, supporting radiation-conscious lymphoma PET/CT. This study was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR) on February 14, 2026 (registration number: ChiCTR2600119037).

articles.title: Demonstrating the False-Positive Paradox in Radiology with Artificial Intelligence: Estimating Clinically Anticipated PPV, FDR, NPV, and FOR of FDA-Cleared Devices Using Performance Metrics from 510(k) Summaries and Prevalences from Local and Published Data.
articles.abstract: The false-positive paradox (FPP) describes the counterintuitive phenomenon whereby a test can achieve high sensitivity and specificity yet still produce mostly false-positive results when applied to low-prevalence populations. This phenomenon is particularly relevant to radiology artificial intelligence (AI), where devices are typically marketed and cleared using diagnostic accuracy metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). However, these metrics do not indicate the proportion of false-positive and false-negative outputs clinicians should expect in local practice. This study estimated the positive predictive value (PPV), false discovery rate (FDR), negative predictive value (NPV), and false omission rate (FOR) for recent Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-cleared radiology AI devices by combining publicly reported 510(k) sensitivity and specificity with local or literature-derived prevalence estimates. Public FDA summaries for 38 radiology AI devices authorized in 2024 or 2025 were reviewed, yielding 57 target pathology entries. Median reported sensitivity, specificity, and ROC-AUC exceeded 90%; nevertheless, clinically anticipated FDRs were often high. For example, a large vessel occlusion detector with 90.6% sensitivity and 88.8% specificity was estimated to have a PPV of 29.3% and an FDR of 70.7% at a prevalence of 4.87%, meaning most positive AI alerts would be false positives. These findings do not evaluate device performance but instead illustrate the FPP in radiology AI. Public 510(k) summaries should consistently report sensitivity, specificity, and test set prevalence so that radiologists and other stakeholders can estimate PPV, FDR, NPV, and FOR for their own patient populations before implementation.

articles.title: Predatory publishing in radiology: advice for early-career researchers.
articles.abstract: Predatory journals typically use practices based on deceit, misleading information, lack of transparency, and the absence of rigorous peer review. Within radiology, such journals frequently publish articles with minimal editorial oversight and limited scientific credibility. The relevance of this issue in radiology has grown as imaging research has expanded rapidly, particularly in artificial intelligence (AI), quantitative imaging, and subspecialty-driven innovation. Given the academic pressure created by the "publish or perish" culture, this environment makes early-career radiologists especially vulnerable to predatory journals that promise rapid publication and high acceptance rates. Predatory journals exploit this environment by sending unsolicited invitations to publish or join editorial boards, frequently using flattering language and promising unrealistic publication timelines. These journals generally lack robust peer review, methodological scrutiny, and transparency and are typically not indexed in established databases such as PubMed, Scopus, or Web of Science. Consequently, articles published in these outlets have reduced visibility, limited citation potential, and minimal impact on radiological science or clinical practice. Furthermore, publication in predatory journals may adversely affect academic reputation and career advancement, as hiring and funding committees increasingly prioritise journal quality and publication integrity. The rapid expansion of radiology research, particularly in diagnostic imaging, interventional radiology, and AI-powered applications, may increase opportunities for the dissemination of low-quality or insufficiently validated evidence through predatory journals. Raising awareness of predatory publishing practices and consistently applying evaluation tools such as the "Think. Check. Submit." framework, are fundamental to safeguarding scientific integrity and ensuring the dissemination of high-quality radiological research. KEY POINTS: Question Predatory publishing is a growing concern in radiology, driven by rising publication pressure and the "publish or perish" culture. Early-career researchers are particularly susceptible to unethical journals that offer rapid publication. Findings Predatory journals frequently bypass rigorous peer review, lack transparency, and are often not indexed in major databases. These journals exploit authors through unsolicited invitations and prioritise profit over scientific quality. Critical relevance statement Avoiding predatory journals is important for protecting research credibility, career progression, and scientific integrity. Publications in these outlets may disseminate unreliable evidence and are often disregarded in academic and clinical evaluations.

Comparative incidence and severity of iodinated and gadolinium-based contrast reactions using actual administration counts: A five-year single-center study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study compared the incidence, severity, and factors associated with adverse reaction severity for iodinated contrast media (ICM) and gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) using actual administration counts. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 849 ICM-related and 193 GBCA-related adverse reaction reports from 2021 to 2025. Denominators were 204,579 contrast-enhanced CT and 66,233 MRI examinations actually performed, excluding angiographic and interventional use. Reaction severity was classified according to American College of Radiology criteria; onset was categorized as immediate or delayed. RESULTS: Adverse reaction incidence was higher with ICM than GBCAs (0.415% vs. 0.291%; odds ratio 1.426, p < 0.001). Iopamidol and gadobutrol had the highest incidence within their respective classes. Among patients with reactions, moderate-to-severe reactions were more frequent with ICM (22.1% vs. 10.9%), whereas severe reaction rates per 10,000 administrations were similar (0.73 vs. 0.91; p = 0.618). Previous reaction history was associated with greater severity among those with reactions. Eleven patients had reactions to both contrast classes, including seven on the same day. Agent-specific comparisons require cautious interpretation owing to potential confounding. CONCLUSION: ICM showed a higher incidence of reported reactions than GBCAs, but severe reaction rates per administration were similar. Prior ICM reaction history may inform GBCA risk assessment; integrated cross-modality screening requires further validation.

articles.title: Fusion of segmental right-lobe IVIM-DWI metrics and GPR for non-invasive assessment of chronic hepatitis B-related hepatic fibrosis: a pilot study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: A segmental intravoxel incoherent motion diffusion-weighted imaging (IVIM-DWI)/gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase-to-platelet ratio (GPR) fusion model was evaluated for the non-invasive assessment of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) fibrosis (controls vs. early; early vs. advanced) and compared with the aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index (APRI) and Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4). METHODS: This retrospective study included 139 participants: 42 healthy controls (HCs), 46 with early hepatic fibrosis (EHF), and 51 with advanced hepatic fibrosis (AHF). IVIM-DWI parameters (apparent diffusion coefficient, slow diffusion component, fast diffusion component, and perfusion fraction) were extracted from segmental analysis of the right hepatic lobe (segments V-VIII). The GPR, APRI, and FIB-4 were calculated from laboratory values. The IVIM + GPR fusion model was developed using logistic regression. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis with bootstrap internal validation. RESULTS: For HCs vs. EHF, FIB-4 achieved the highest area under the curve [AUC; 0.911, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.844-0.969) followed by APRI (0.843, 95% CI: 0.755-0.923). The IVIM + GPR fusion model (AUC = 0.745, 95% CI: 0.643-0.847) outperformed IVIM alone (AUC = 0.652) and GPR alone (AUC = 0.730) but did not outperform APRI or FIB-4. For EHF vs. AHF, the IVIM + GPR fusion model (AUC = 0.698) was comparable to APRI (0.573) and FIB-4 (0.637), with no significant differences among methods. CONCLUSION: FIB-4/APRI outperformed the fusion model for controls vs. early fibrosis, whereas fusion added no value over GPR for early vs. advanced fibrosis. In the absence of a biopsy-proven S0 CHB group, HCs vs. EHF discriminates between HCs and established fibrosis rather than detecting incident fibrosis. The model should be considered, at most, a supplementary, opportunistic adjunct during abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) rather than a replacement for FIB-4/APRI. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: The GPR uses only gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase and platelets, making it practical in resource- limited settings. The fusion model may provide supplementary, opportunistic information during abdominal MRI or when serum markers are confounded by extrahepatic factors, but it should remain complementary pending validation in larger cohorts; FIB-4 and APRI remain first-line where laboratory panels are available.

articles.title: Contrast-enhanced mammography findings of idiopathic granulomatous mastitis: a retrospective analysis of seventy histopathologically proven cases.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to characterize the contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) findings of histopathologically confirmed idiopathic granulomatous mastitis (IGM), compare isolated mass and non-mass enhancement (NME) phenotypes, and explore the cumulative burden of malignancy-mimicking imaging features using an exploratory malignancy-mimicking feature score (MMFS). METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included 70 women with histopathologically confirmed IGM who underwent CEM between 2021 and 2024. Imaging findings were reviewed in consensus by two breast radiologists according to the Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System Manual (2025 edition). Lesion morphology, enhancement characteristics, temporal enhancement patterns, conspicuity, and associated imaging findings were recorded. Patients with isolated mass lesions and isolated NMEs were compared. The MMFS was calculated from 12 predefined malignancy-mimicking CEM features, including moderate/high enhancement conspicuity, plateau/washout temporal enhancement patterns, suspicious mass morphology, segmental/linear NME distribution, and associated findings, such as skin thickening and axillary lymphadenopathy. RESULTS: The mean patient age was 41.7 ± 8.7 years, and the mean lesion size was 57.3 ± 26.8 mm. NME was the predominant imaging presentation (55.7%), and 14.3% of patients demonstrated both mass and NMEs. Contrast enhancement was present in all lesions, with heterogeneous enhancement (44.3%), high enhancement conspicuity (44.3%), and axillary lymphadenopathy (47.1%) being common findings. Compared with isolated mass lesions, isolated NMEs were significantly larger (median = 70 vs. 50 mm; P = 0.017) and more frequently associated with skin thickening (46.2% vs. 9.5%; P = 0.004). The mean MMFS was 3.41 ± 1.66. All patients demonstrated at least one malignancy-mimicking imaging feature; 90.0% had two or more features, and 65.7% had three or more features. CONCLUSION: IGM demonstrates a broad spectrum of CEM findings, including multiple imaging features conventionally considered suspicious for malignancy. NME is the predominant imaging phenotype and is associated with larger lesion size and more frequent skin thickening than isolated mass lesions. The high cumulative burden of malignancy-mimicking imaging features highlights the diagnostic challenge posed by IGM on CEM. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: IGM frequently mimics breast cancer on CEM because multiple suspicious imaging features often coexist within the same lesion. Familiarity with the CEM spectrum of IGM may facilitate the appropriate interpretation of suspicious findings and contribute to informed patient management.
